Hello, friends,

I'm continuing to walk you through the Rho Agenda novels, one book at a time, and to do it without spoiling the turns that should take you by surprise. Last time I wrote my note on Once Dead, Book One of The Rho Agenda Inception, the spy-thriller door into this universe. This week I want to take you into Book Two: Dead Wrong, which came out in 2015.

Gregory and Price are hunted. The conspiracy is larger than either of them.

That is the door into this novel. Jack “the Ripper” Gregory and Janet Price walked away from each other at the end of Once Dead. This is their reunion... an extremely uncomfortable one. The people who resurrected Jack have decided he is more useful dead — or leashed. This one is a globe-spanning sci-fi thriller, and it is the second novel in my Rho Agenda Inception trilogy.

In this book, it becomes increasingly clear to Jack that the mind he hosts is hostile. The symbiotic relationship subjects him to increasingly disturbing premonitions and compulsions. He struggles to retain his sanity.

In the midst of that struggle, he is hired for a suicide mission. He is to journey to South America and rescue an imprisoned shaman. At stake is the Sun Staff, an ancient alien artifact that, in the wrong hands, will alter the course of human history. The National Security Agency and a gang of neo-fascists are already on his trail. Neither group plans to let him live. I will not tell you more about that hunt, or about the artifact, than the book itself puts on the table at the start.

He has to confront two possibilities: either he is tightly coupled to mankind's destiny, or he is losing his mind. And when an NSA agent throws him a lifeline, Jack fears that if he grabs it, he will pull her into his death spiral. The alien being who shares his mind may leave him no choice.

One of my favorite chapters is the shortest in Dead Wrong. Here it is in its entirety:

The mind-worm had been called by many names, among them, Anchanchu, the soul bane. Loosely translated, it meant The Rider. Although humans thought of it as a demonic being from their various religious traditions, the truth was something far stranger. It was an entity beyond the four dimensions that compose space-time, able to observe all possible timelines but, until it had discovered the human race, unable to experience any of them, its existence a frustrating hell from which humanity’s arrival on the cosmic stage had offered release.

Anchanchu had learned that, as a human straddled the life-death threshold, it could establish a parasitic link to that person’s limbic system. It required the host’s cooperation but, once accepted, it could stimulate the human’s physical responses far more effectively than a doctor’s adrenaline injection or electric paddles. If the body was not too badly damaged, Anchanchu could shove its host back across the life-death boundary.

The mind-worm’s limbic attachment enabled it to feel human emotion, to experience the world through its host’s senses, to amplify its host’s feelings and bodily responses. But Anchanchu’s lack of connection to the higher brain functions meant it was unable to sense its host’s thoughts.

Anchanchu knew its hosts better than they knew themselves. It understood what drove them. And with its ability to sense what was coming, it was easy to see the paths along which their amplified passions would carry them. Breaking a new host was different in every case. With some it was as simple as amping-up specific desires. Though some struggled to resist its siren call and to maintain their sense of self-control, even the most strong-willed generally succumbed within months.

As difficult as it was for the mind-worm to accept, in the months since Jack Gregory’s deathbed acceptance, the man continued fighting to reestablish his self-control. It was a new experience, one that Anchanchu found both thrilling and terrifying.

It was time to apply the bloody spurs that would break this stallion to rein, once and for all.

What is the Rider pushing him toward? Why is he bound to the fate of a shaman and an ancient artifact? Is he tightly coupled to mankind's destiny, or is he coming apart? Those are the questions I want you to carry into the book. I will not answer them here.

Where it fits in the Rho Agenda

Dead Wrong is Book Two of The Rho Agenda Inception. Once Dead opens that spy-thriller trilogy; Dead Shift completes it. Together the three books follow Jack and Janet Price — a CIA assassin and the partner who can keep up with him — and open the Rho universe from the shadows.

This is the first hard link to the Rho Agenda science-fiction series. In my mind, this is the genesis of everything that follows.

If you want every knife in the drawer, the order I recommend is this: the Inception trilogy (Once Dead, Dead Wrong, and Dead Shift), then the original Rho Agenda trilogy (The Second Ship, Immune, and Wormhole), then Assimilation (The Kasari Nexus, The Altreian Enigma, The Meridian Ascent), then Singularity, which opens with The Ripper's Son.

There is more than one correct door. If you have just finished Once Dead, Dead Wrong is the next book in that trilogy. If you came to these stories through The Second Ship, you can step into Inception whenever you want the assassin's story from the beginning.

Either way, hang on for this ride... It's about to get wilder.

If you would like to read it, you can find Dead Wrong at thesecondship.net/books/dead-wrong.

Richard
